_about: Page-specific slot text for the 20 VELOCITY_DISAMBIGUATOR_20 comparison pages. The retired program that wrote them filled four of five decision sections and the whole comparison table with the same words on every page (Search Readiness q1, 17 Nov 2026: 20 of 20 pages template filler). Applied by scripts/content/apply_disambiguator_specifics.js. No figures, no prices, no outcome claims: each line says what the two options are for and what to check, in words only that page can use.
boilerplate_sentence: Compare the categories, verify the current source, and continue to {host} for the complete canonical next step.

/adhd-evaluation-vs-neuropsychological-e.core_q: What is the core difference between an ADHD evaluation and a neuropsychological evaluation?
rows: Whether attention and activity symptoms meet ADHD criteria
How memory, language, attention, reasoning and other domains work together
Psychiatrist, psychologist, pediatrician or other licensed clinician
Interviews, rating scales and history, sometimes brief testing
A longer battery of standardized tests across many domains
When learning, memory or neurological concerns also need answers
When the only question is a straightforward ADHD diagnosis

sections.q: When is a focused ADHD evaluation enough?
sections.a: An ADHD evaluation is usually enough when the concern is attention, impulsivity or restlessness alone, there is no head injury or medical condition in the history, and school or work problems line up with those symptoms.
checklist: Gather rating scales from more than one setting, such as home and school.
Ask whether the clinician screens for anxiety, sleep and mood problems that can look like ADHD.

sections.q: When does a neuropsychological evaluation make more sense?
sections.a: A neuropsychological evaluation fits when ADHD questions overlap with learning disability, memory loss, a seizure disorder, brain injury, or a past evaluation that did not explain the problem. It maps strengths and weaknesses rather than giving one label.
checklist: List every concern beyond attention before the intake call.
Ask whether the report will include school or workplace recommendations.

sections.q: What should I ask before booking either evaluation?
sections.a: Ask what question the evaluation is meant to answer, who will interpret the results, how long the testing takes, whether insurance needs a referral, and whether the final report will be written for a school, an employer or a prescriber.
checklist: Confirm the evaluator's license type and testing experience with your age group.
Ask how long after testing the written report arrives.

sections.q: Who should I contact first?
sections.a: Start with the primary care clinician or pediatrician, who can screen for medical causes and refer. For a broad or complex picture, ask for a neuropsychologist; for a focused question, a psychiatrist or psychologist may be enough.
checklist: Ask the primary care office which local evaluators accept your plan.
Check wait lists early, since testing slots can fill months ahead.

/civil-surgeon-vs-panel-physician/.core_q: What is the core difference between a civil surgeon and a panel physician?
rows: Outside the United States, before the visa interview
Someone adjusting status to permanent resident from within the U.S.
Someone applying for an immigrant visa at a U.S. embassy or consulate
Form I-693, sealed and submitted to USCIS
Exam results sent to the consulate for the visa case

sections.q: When do I need a civil surgeon?
sections.a: You need a civil surgeon when you are applying to adjust status to permanent resident while living in the United States. Only a doctor USCIS has designated as a civil surgeon can complete and sign Form I-693.
checklist: Confirm the doctor appears in the USCIS civil surgeon locator.
Bring your vaccination records and photo ID to the exam.

sections.q: When do I need a panel physician?
sections.a: You need a panel physician when your immigrant visa interview will take place at a U.S. embassy or consulate abroad. The Department of State lists the panel physicians each post accepts, and a doctor outside that list cannot do the exam.
checklist: Use the panel physician list for the embassy or consulate handling your case.
Follow the post's own instructions on when to book the exam.

sections.q: What should I check before booking the exam?
sections.a: Check that the doctor is designated for your situation, what the exam fee covers, whether vaccines and blood tests are billed separately, and how the doctor will deliver the sealed form or results.
checklist: Ask whether chest X-rays or blood tests are done on site.
Ask how long results take to return if more tests are needed.

sections.q: Where do I find a designated doctor?
sections.a: Inside the U.S., search the USCIS Find a Civil Surgeon tool by ZIP code. Abroad, use the panel physician list on the embassy or consulate website for your interview location.
checklist: Call ahead to confirm the doctor still holds the designation.
Ask about appointment availability before your filing or interview date.

/comparative-negligence-vs-contributory-.core_q: What is the core difference between comparative and contributory negligence?
rows: Recovery is reduced by your share of fault
Any fault of your own can bar recovery
Used by most U.S. states in pure or modified form
Used by only a few jurisdictions
Pure systems and modified systems with a fault threshold
Exceptions such as last clear chance in some places
The law of the state where the claim is brought
The law of the state where the claim is brought

sections.q: How does comparative negligence affect a claim?
sections.a: Under comparative negligence, a person who was partly at fault can still recover, but the amount is reduced by their share of fault. Modified versions stop recovery once the person's fault reaches the state's threshold.
checklist: Find out whether your state uses a pure or a modified rule.
Keep evidence that shows how the other party contributed to the accident.

sections.q: How does contributory negligence affect a claim?
sections.a: Under contributory negligence, a person found even slightly at fault can be barred from recovering. Because the rule is strict, the facts about who did what, and any exception the jurisdiction recognizes, carry more weight.
checklist: Confirm whether the accident state is one of the few that keep this rule.
Write down your own account of the accident while it is fresh.

sections.q: What should I check about my state's rule?
sections.a: Check which fault rule the accident state uses, whether a different rule applies to the type of claim, how fault is assigned among several parties, and the filing deadline, since the rule and the deadline both come from state law.
checklist: Read the state court or legislature summary of the fault rule.
Note the statute of limitations for your claim type.

sections.q: Who can explain how the rule applies to me?
sections.a: A licensed attorney in the state where the accident happened can explain how the fault rule applies to your facts. The state bar association can confirm a lawyer's license; this site does not endorse or recommend any lawyer.
checklist: Verify any lawyer's license with the state bar.
Ask how fault will be investigated before you sign anything.

/cosmetic-vs-general-dentistry/.core_q: What is the core difference between cosmetic and general dentistry?
rows: Changing how teeth and smiles look
Often limited when the work is purely for looks
Preventive and basic care often covered by dental plans
The core of general dental practice

sections.q: When does cosmetic dentistry fit?
sections.a: Cosmetic dentistry fits when the teeth are healthy and the goal is to change color, shape or alignment for appearance. It works best after decay or gum disease has been treated, since cosmetic work placed over untreated problems can fail.
checklist: Ask to see before-and-after photos of the dentist's own cases.
Ask which parts of the plan are cosmetic and which are restorative.

sections.q: When should I start with general dentistry?
sections.a: Start with general dentistry when there is pain, a broken tooth, bleeding gums, or it has been a long time since a checkup. A general dentist diagnoses and treats health problems first and can refer for cosmetic or specialty care.
checklist: Book an exam and cleaning before planning any cosmetic work.
Ask for a written treatment plan that ranks health needs first.

sections.q: What should I check before cosmetic work?
sections.a: Check whether the dentist has training in the procedure, how long the result is expected to last, whether it removes natural tooth structure, what upkeep it needs, and what the plan says about redoing work that chips or stains.
checklist: Ask whether the procedure is reversible.
Ask for the written cost of each step and any lab fees.

sections.q: How do I find the right dentist for this?
sections.a: A general dentist handles most care and many cosmetic services. For complex smile work, ask how many similar cases the dentist has done. Your state dental board confirms that any dentist holds a current license.
checklist: Check the license on your state dental board website.
Ask whether consultations for cosmetic work are free or charged.

/dental-implant-vs-bridge-vs-denture/.core_q: How do a dental implant, a bridge and a denture differ?
rows: A post placed in the jawbone
A bridge is anchored on neighboring teeth; a denture rests on the gums
Does not rely on neighboring teeth
A bridge usually needs crowns on the teeth beside the gap
Yes, and sometimes a bone graft first
No surgery for most bridges and dentures
Bridge no; denture yes, taken out for cleaning

sections.q: When does a dental implant fit?
sections.a: An implant fits when there is enough healthy jawbone, the gums are healthy, and the person can go through minor surgery and a healing period. Smoking and some medical conditions can affect healing, so the dentist reviews health history first.
checklist: Ask whether imaging shows enough bone for an implant.
Ask who places the implant and who makes the crown on top.

sections.q: When do a bridge or a denture fit better?
sections.a: A bridge can fit when the teeth beside the gap are strong and already need crowns. A denture can fit when several or all teeth are missing, or when surgery is not a good option. Both are usually finished faster than an implant.
checklist: Ask how the bridge will affect the teeth beside the gap.
Ask how often a denture needs relining or replacing.

sections.q: What should I compare before choosing?
sections.a: Compare how long each option is expected to last, what upkeep it needs, how it affects chewing and nearby teeth, how many visits it takes, and what your plan pays toward each one, since plans treat these three very differently.
checklist: Get a written estimate for each option, including follow-up visits.
Ask your plan which of the three it covers and at what level.

sections.q: Who should I see about tooth replacement?
sections.a: A general dentist can examine the gap and explain options. Implants may involve an oral surgeon or periodontist for placement and a prosthodontist or general dentist for the tooth on top. Your state dental board confirms each license.
checklist: Ask which providers will be involved at each step.
Confirm each provider's license with the state dental board.

/dental-insurance-vs-medical-insurance/.core_q: What is the core difference between dental insurance and medical insurance?
rows: Cleanings, fillings, crowns and other routine dental care
Illness, injury and hospital care, including some mouth-related surgery
An annual maximum the plan will pay
An out-of-pocket maximum the member pays
When it may cover mouth care
Accidental injury, some oral surgery, or care tied to a medical condition

sections.q: When does dental insurance usually pay?
sections.a: Dental insurance usually pays for preventive care, fillings, crowns, root canals and similar treatment, often with waiting periods, frequency limits and a yearly maximum. Cosmetic work is usually excluded.
checklist: Read your plan's yearly maximum and waiting periods.
Ask the office to send a pre-treatment estimate for large work.

sections.q: When might medical insurance pay for mouth care?
sections.a: Medical insurance may pay when a mouth problem is caused by an accident, needs hospital care, or is tied to a medical condition, such as some jaw surgery or tooth removal before cancer treatment. Coverage depends on the plan's rules.
checklist: Ask whether the office can bill medical insurance first.
Ask your medical plan whether the procedure needs prior approval.

sections.q: What should I check before treatment?
sections.a: Check which plan the office will bill, whether the treatment needs prior approval, whether the provider is in network for that plan, and what you will owe after both plans pay. Medicaid dental benefits for adults vary by state.
checklist: Get the estimate in writing from the billing office.
Check your state's Medicaid dental benefits if you are enrolled.

sections.q: Who can help sort out coverage?
sections.a: The dental office's billing staff can check benefits with both plans. Your plans' member services lines can explain coverage rules, and state Medicaid offices explain adult dental benefits where they exist.
checklist: Call member services with the procedure code in hand.
Keep a record of who you spoke with and what they said.

/dentist-vs-oral-surgeon-vs-endodontist/.core_q: How do a general dentist, an oral surgeon and an endodontist differ?
rows: Overall oral health, prevention and routine treatment
Oral surgeon: surgery of the mouth and jaw; endodontist: the inside of the tooth
Exams, cleanings, fillings, crowns, simple extractions
Oral surgeon: complex extractions, implants, jaw surgery; endodontist: root canals
Often by referral from a general dentist

sections.q: When is a general dentist the right first stop?
sections.a: A general dentist is the right first stop for checkups, cavities, chipped teeth and most tooth pain. They diagnose the problem, treat many cases themselves and refer to a specialist when the case needs more.
checklist: Describe where the pain is and what makes it worse.
Ask whether the dentist does root canals or extractions in house.

sections.q: When do I need an oral surgeon or an endodontist?
sections.a: See an oral surgeon for impacted wisdom teeth, complex extractions, implants or jaw problems. See an endodontist for a difficult root canal, a retreatment, or tooth pain whose source is hard to find.
checklist: Ask the referring dentist to send X-rays ahead of the visit.
Ask the specialist what sedation options they offer.

sections.q: What should I check before a specialist visit?
sections.a: Check whether your plan needs a referral, whether the specialist is in network, what the consultation costs, and whether the treatment can happen on the same day or needs a second visit.
checklist: Get a written estimate before treatment starts.
Ask who handles follow-up if problems come back.

sections.q: How do I find the right provider?
sections.a: Ask your general dentist for a referral first, since they know the case. Specialty groups such as the American Association of Endodontists list members, and your state dental board confirms any dentist's license.
checklist: Confirm the license on the state dental board site.
Ask your plan for in-network specialists near you.

/i-693-rejection-vs-denial-vs-rfe/.core_q: How do an I-693 rejection, a denial and an RFE differ?
rows: Rejection: at intake, before review; RFE: during review
Rejection: filing not accepted as submitted; RFE: more evidence needed
Missing signature, unsealed envelope, outdated form edition, missing vaccine record
No timely or adequate response to an RFE, or other ineligibility
Refile correctly, or answer the RFE by its deadline
Read the notice for motion, appeal or refiling options

sections.q: What does an RFE about Form I-693 mean?
sections.a: A Request for Evidence means USCIS is reviewing the case but needs more, such as a new or corrected I-693, missing vaccination records, or a form whose envelope seal was broken. The notice names what is needed and the deadline.
checklist: Read the RFE line by line and list each item requested.
Book the civil surgeon early if a new exam is needed.

sections.q: What does a denial mean, and what can follow?
sections.a: A denial is a decision against the application. The notice explains the reason and whether a motion to reopen or reconsider, an appeal, or a new filing is possible. Deadlines for those options are short.
checklist: Note the date on the denial notice right away.
Read which options the notice lists and their deadlines.

sections.q: What should I check on the notice?
sections.a: Check the notice type, the receipt number, the deadline, the exact items requested, and the mailing address or upload instructions. A rejection notice also states why the filing was not accepted.
checklist: Compare the form edition date with the one USCIS currently accepts.
Keep copies of everything sent back to USCIS.

sections.q: Who can help with a response?
sections.a: A USCIS-designated civil surgeon can redo or correct the medical form. An immigration attorney or a Department of Justice accredited representative can advise on the legal response to an RFE or a denial.
checklist: Use the USCIS civil surgeon locator for a new exam.
Check that any representative is licensed or DOJ accredited.

/invisalign-vs-braces-vs-clear-aligners/.core_q: How do Invisalign, braces and other clear aligners differ?
rows: Yes, taken out to eat and clean
Yes, worn most of the day to work
No, works whether or not you remember
Mild to moderate cases; some complex cases with attachments
Orthodontist or dentist, in person or partly remote with some brands
Orthodontist or dentist, with regular in-person adjustments

sections.q: When do clear aligners fit?
sections.a: Clear aligners fit mild to moderate crowding or spacing in people who will wear the trays most of the day and keep them clean. Invisalign is one brand; other aligner brands work in a similar way with different supervision models.
checklist: Ask whether the plan includes refinement trays and retainers.
Ask how often you will be seen in person.

sections.q: When do braces fit better?
sections.a: Braces fit complex tooth movement, bite problems and cases where wearing removable trays would be hard. Because they stay on, they keep working without daily effort from the patient.
checklist: Ask how many adjustment visits the plan needs.
Ask which foods to avoid with brackets.

sections.q: What should I check before choosing?
sections.a: Check who diagnoses and supervises the case, whether X-rays are taken first, how long treatment should take, what happens if teeth do not track, and whether retainers after treatment are included in the price.
checklist: Get the full written cost, including retainers.
Ask about the refund policy for at-home aligner programs.

sections.q: Who should I see about straightening teeth?
sections.a: An orthodontist is a dentist with specialty training in moving teeth and can offer both braces and aligners. Many general dentists offer aligners too. Your state dental board confirms the license.
checklist: Ask how many aligner cases the provider has finished.
Get a second opinion if only one option is offered.

/neuropsych-eval-vs-iq-test-vs-psych-eva.core_q: How do a neuropsych evaluation, a psychological evaluation and an IQ test differ?
rows: Many thinking skills and how they relate to brain function
Psych evaluation: mood, behavior, personality; IQ test: general reasoning ability
Psych evaluation varies; an IQ test is one session
Brain injury, memory concerns, complex learning problems
Mental health diagnosis, or a single ability score
A profile of strengths and weaknesses with recommendations
A diagnosis or a set of scores

sections.q: When is a neuropsych evaluation the right choice?
sections.a: A neuropsych evaluation is the right choice when the concern involves memory, attention, language or problem solving linked to a medical or neurological condition, or when earlier testing left questions unanswered.
checklist: Bring medical records and past test reports.
Ask which thinking areas the battery will cover.

sections.q: When is a psychological evaluation or an IQ test enough?
sections.a: A psychological evaluation can be enough when the questions are about mood, anxiety, behavior or personality. An IQ test alone fits when a program or school needs one ability score, but it does not explain why someone struggles.
checklist: Ask whether the evaluation will include a diagnosis.
Ask whether an IQ score alone meets the program's requirement.

sections.q: What should I ask before scheduling?
sections.a: Ask what question the testing will answer, which tests will be used, who interprets the results, whether insurance covers it as medical or educational testing, and who the written report is meant for.
checklist: Confirm the evaluator's license and specialty.
Ask how long the report takes after testing.

sections.q: Who does each kind of testing?
sections.a: Neuropsychologists perform neuropsych evaluations. Licensed psychologists perform psychological evaluations and give IQ tests. School psychologists may test for school purposes. State licensing boards confirm each license.
checklist: Ask the referring doctor which type of evaluator fits.
Check the license with the state psychology board.

/personal-injury-vs-workers-comp/.core_q: What is the core difference between a personal injury claim and a workers compensation claim?
rows: The at-fault party or their insurer
Yes, you must show another party was at fault
Generally no, a work-related injury is the trigger
Medical bills, lost income and pain and suffering
Medical care and partial wage replacement under state schedules
Through negotiation or a civil court
Through the state workers compensation system

sections.q: When does a personal injury claim apply?
sections.a: A personal injury claim applies when someone else's carelessness caused the injury, such as a car crash, a fall on another's property, or a defective product. You must show fault, and state deadlines apply.
checklist: Collect photos, police reports and witness names.
Write down the date and place of the injury.

sections.q: When does workers compensation apply?
sections.a: Workers compensation applies when an employee is hurt on the job or gets sick from work. It usually pays regardless of fault, but in exchange the worker generally cannot sue the employer for that injury.
checklist: Report the injury to your employer in writing quickly.
Ask for the employer's workers compensation insurer name.

sections.q: Can both apply to the same injury?
sections.a: Sometimes. If a third party, such as another driver or an equipment maker, caused a work injury, a worker may have a workers compensation claim and a separate claim against that party. Reimbursement rules between the two vary by state.
checklist: List everyone involved in how the injury happened.
Check your state's reporting and filing deadlines for both.

sections.q: Who can explain my options?
sections.a: Your state workers compensation agency explains the claims process. A licensed attorney in your state can explain third-party claims. The state bar confirms a lawyer's license; this site does not endorse or recommend any lawyer.
checklist: Find your state's workers compensation agency website.
Confirm on the state bar's website that any lawyer you speak with is licensed.

/prp-vs-microneedling-for-hair-loss/.core_q: What is the core difference between PRP and microneedling for hair loss?
rows: Drawing blood, concentrating platelets and injecting them into the scalp
Rolling or stamping fine needles over the scalp to create tiny punctures
A clinician, since it uses a blood draw and injections
A clinician, or a home device for shallower needling
A series of injection sessions, then maintenance
Repeated sessions, often combined with a topical treatment
How the platelet preparation is made and how many sessions are planned
Needle depth, device cleaning, and what is applied after

sections.q: When might PRP be considered?
sections.a: PRP may be considered for pattern hair loss when a clinician has confirmed the diagnosis and ruled out thyroid, iron or medication causes. Preparation methods differ between clinics, which makes results hard to compare.
checklist: Ask which preparation system the clinic uses.
Ask how they will measure whether it is working.

sections.q: When might microneedling be considered?
sections.a: Microneedling may be considered for pattern hair loss, often alongside a topical treatment such as minoxidil. Clinic devices reach deeper than home rollers, and infection risk rises when needles are not sterile.
checklist: Ask about needle depth and sterilization.
Ask whether to pause topical treatments around sessions.

sections.q: What should I check before starting either?
sections.a: Check the diagnosis first, then ask what evidence the clinic relies on, how many sessions the plan includes, the total written cost, the side effects, and whether the treatment is combined with medication.
checklist: Get the full session plan and price in writing.
Take dated scalp photos before the first session.

sections.q: Who should evaluate the hair loss first?
sections.a: A dermatologist can diagnose the type of hair loss and check for medical causes before any procedure. Clinics that offer PRP or microneedling should explain who performs the procedure and their license.
checklist: Book a diagnosis visit before buying a package.
Confirm the license of the person doing the procedure.

/school-iep-evaluation-vs-private-neurop.core_q: What is the core difference between a school IEP evaluation and a private neuropsych evaluation?
rows: The public school district, at no cost to the family
The family or their health insurance
Whether the child qualifies for special education services
What is causing the difficulty and what helps, including medical diagnoses
The IEP team under federal and state special education rules
The family decides how to use the report
No, the school must consider it but does not have to adopt it

sections.q: When should I ask the school to evaluate?
sections.a: Ask the school to evaluate when a child struggles with learning, attention or behavior at school despite support. A written request starts timelines under special education law, and the evaluation is free to the family.
checklist: Send the evaluation request to the school in writing and keep a copy.
Ask which areas the school plans to test.

sections.q: When does a private neuropsych evaluation add value?
sections.a: A private neuropsych evaluation adds value when the family wants a medical diagnosis, a deeper look at memory, attention or language, or a second view after a school evaluation they disagree with.
checklist: Ask whether the evaluator writes school-ready recommendations.
Ask whether insurance covers the testing.

sections.q: What if I disagree with the school's evaluation?
sections.a: Families who disagree with a school evaluation can ask for an independent educational evaluation at public expense. The district must either pay for one or start a hearing to defend its own evaluation.
checklist: Put the disagreement and the request in writing.
Ask the district for its evaluator criteria.

sections.q: Who can guide the process?
sections.a: The school's special education office handles the school evaluation. Each state has a federally funded Parent Training and Information Center that helps families for free. Neuropsychologists perform private evaluations.
checklist: Find your state's Parent Training and Information Center.
Confirm a private evaluator's license with the state board.

/settlement-demand-vs-lawsuit-filing/.core_q: What is the core difference between a settlement demand and filing a lawsuit?
rows: A written request to the insurer or at-fault party to pay
A formal complaint filed with a court
Does not stop the statute of limitations
Filing on time preserves the claim
Court rules, discovery and possibly trial
Yes, court filings are generally public

sections.q: When does a settlement demand make sense?
sections.a: A settlement demand makes sense once medical treatment has stabilized and the costs are known. It lists the injuries, bills and lost income, and asks for a specific amount, starting a negotiation.
checklist: Gather medical bills, records and wage loss proof.
Keep copies of every letter sent to the insurer.

sections.q: When does filing a lawsuit become necessary?
sections.a: Filing a lawsuit becomes necessary when the insurer will not negotiate fairly or the statute of limitations is close. Filing preserves the claim, and settlement talks can continue after the case is filed.
checklist: Find the statute of limitations for your claim and state.
Mark the deadline on a calendar well ahead of time.

sections.q: What should I check before either step?
sections.a: Check the filing deadline, whether all treatment is finished, the insurance policy limits, any liens from health insurers, and whether a release in a settlement would end all future claims.
checklist: Read any release carefully before signing.
Ask whether health insurers must be repaid from a settlement.

sections.q: Who can explain the choice?
sections.a: A licensed attorney in the state where the injury happened can explain deadlines and court rules. The state bar confirms a lawyer's license; this site does not endorse or recommend any lawyer.
checklist: Verify a lawyer's license with the state bar.
Ask how fees and costs are charged before signing.

/ssdi-eval-vs-school-iep-eval-vs-forensi.core_q: Which decision does each of these three evaluations serve?
rows: School IEP team, or a court or attorney for forensic work
School: eligibility for special education; forensic: a legal question
SSA may order and pay for a consultative exam
School: the district; forensic: usually the requesting party
School team, or judges, lawyers and the court

sections.q: When is an SSDI evaluation needed?
sections.a: An SSDI evaluation is needed when Social Security needs more medical evidence to decide a disability claim. SSA may schedule a consultative exam, and treating providers' records also carry weight.
checklist: Keep every SSA letter and appointment notice.
Bring a list of medications and treating providers to the exam.

sections.q: When are school or forensic evaluations needed?
sections.a: A school IEP evaluation is needed to decide special education eligibility for a student. A forensic evaluation is needed when a court or attorney asks a legal question, such as competency, custody or injury in a lawsuit.
checklist: Ask who requested the evaluation and who receives the report.
Ask whether the evaluator will testify.

sections.q: What should I ask any evaluator?
sections.a: Ask who the report is for, what question it answers, who pays, whether you can get a copy, and how confidentiality works, because forensic reports can go to the court rather than to you.
checklist: Ask for the evaluator's credentials in writing.
Ask about confidentiality before the first session.

sections.q: Where do I start?
sections.a: For SSDI, start with the Social Security Administration. For school evaluations, start with the school's special education office. For forensic work, the attorney or court that needs it usually arranges the evaluator.
checklist: Use SSA's website or local office for SSDI questions.
Put school evaluation requests in writing.

/telehealth-trt-vs-in-person-trt/.core_q: What is the core difference between telehealth TRT and in-person TRT?
rows: Limited or none; may rely on outside labs
Ordered at a partner lab or home kit
Often drawn in the office or a nearby lab
Testosterone is a controlled substance; telehealth prescribing rules apply
Must be licensed in the state where you are located

sections.q: When can telehealth TRT work?
sections.a: Telehealth TRT can work when labs confirm low testosterone on more than one morning test, the clinician is licensed in your state, and the service orders regular follow-up labs to check blood counts and hormone levels.
checklist: Confirm the clinician's license in your state.
Ask what lab tests are required before a prescription.

sections.q: When is in-person TRT the better fit?
sections.a: In-person TRT is the better fit when an exam is needed, such as checking for other causes of symptoms, when there are heart, prostate or sleep apnea concerns, or when injections are given in the office.
checklist: Ask whether the clinic gives injections on site.
Bring a full medication list to the first visit.

sections.q: What should I check with either option?
sections.a: Check how the diagnosis is confirmed, which labs are monitored and how often, how prescriptions are filled, what the monthly cost includes, and whether the service screens for fertility goals before prescribing.
checklist: Ask how often follow-up labs are drawn.
Ask how to stop treatment safely if needed.

sections.q: Who should prescribe TRT?
sections.a: A licensed clinician, such as a primary care doctor, urologist or endocrinologist, should confirm the diagnosis and prescribe. State medical boards confirm licenses, and pharmacies must be licensed to dispense.
checklist: Verify the prescriber with the state medical board.
Confirm the pharmacy is licensed.

/trt-vs-clomiphene-vs-enclomiphene/.core_q: How do TRT, clomiphene and enclomiphene differ?
rows: Signals the brain to make the body produce more
Aims to keep the body's own production going
FDA-approved testosterone products for diagnosed deficiency
Clomiphene used off label in men; enclomiphene not FDA approved

sections.q: When is TRT considered?
sections.a: TRT is considered when repeated morning blood tests confirm low testosterone along with symptoms, and the person is not trying to conceive soon. It needs ongoing monitoring of blood counts and hormone levels.
checklist: Confirm low testosterone on more than one morning test.
Tell the clinician about any plans to have children.

sections.q: When are clomiphene or enclomiphene considered?
sections.a: Clomiphene may be considered off label when fertility matters and the cause is in the brain's signaling. Enclomiphene is not FDA approved; products sold as enclomiphene are often compounded, so quality and regulation differ.
checklist: Ask whether the drug is FDA approved for your use.
Ask where a compounded product comes from.

sections.q: What should I check before starting?
sections.a: Check the diagnosis, fertility plans, what monitoring is needed, possible side effects such as vision changes with clomiphene, and whether the pharmacy is licensed and inspected.
checklist: Ask for the monitoring schedule in writing.
Verify the pharmacy's license.

sections.q: Who should guide this decision?
sections.a: A urologist, endocrinologist or reproductive specialist can weigh fertility goals and hormone causes. State medical boards confirm prescriber licenses.
checklist: Ask for a referral if fertility is a priority.
Verify the prescriber's license.

/trt-vs-hair-loss-treatment/.core_q: How do TRT and hair-loss treatment relate?
rows: Can speed pattern hair loss in people prone to it
Aims to slow loss or regrow hair
Minoxidil, finasteride, procedures such as PRP

sections.q: When does TRT come into the hair question?
sections.a: TRT comes into the hair question when someone on testosterone notices thinning, or someone with thinning wonders if hormones are the cause. Testosterone can convert to DHT, which drives pattern loss in people genetically prone to it.
checklist: Note when thinning started relative to any hormone treatment.
Bring recent lab results to the visit.

sections.q: When is hair-loss treatment the focus?
sections.a: Hair-loss treatment is the focus when the pattern looks genetic, or when shedding follows illness, stress, iron deficiency or thyroid problems. Treatment depends on which type of loss is present.
checklist: Ask for a diagnosis of the type of hair loss.
Ask whether thyroid and iron tests are needed.

sections.q: Can both be used together?
sections.a: Some people on TRT also use hair-loss treatments. Finasteride and similar drugs change how testosterone is converted, so the prescriber should know about both treatments and monitor for side effects.
checklist: Tell each prescriber about all hormone and hair medicines.
Ask how side effects will be monitored.

sections.q: Who should I see?
sections.a: A dermatologist diagnoses hair loss. A primary care doctor, urologist or endocrinologist manages testosterone. State medical boards confirm each clinician's license.
checklist: Book the dermatologist for a scalp exam.
Share notes between both clinicians.

/trt-vs-peptide-therapy/.core_q: What is the core difference between TRT and peptide therapy?
rows: Testosterone given to replace low levels
Short chains of amino acids marketed for many goals
Many marketed peptides are not FDA approved for these uses
Often sold without a specific diagnosis
Often compounding pharmacies, where FDA has restricted some peptides

sections.q: When does TRT fit?
sections.a: TRT fits when repeated morning blood tests confirm low testosterone with symptoms, and the person is not planning to conceive soon. It is prescribed and monitored with regular lab work.
checklist: Confirm the diagnosis with repeated morning tests.
Ask about the monitoring schedule.

sections.q: Where does peptide therapy stand?
sections.a: Peptide therapy covers many different products. Some peptides are FDA-approved drugs for specific conditions, but many sold for anti-aging, muscle or recovery lack approval for those uses, and FDA has limited compounding of some.
checklist: Ask for the exact peptide name and its approval status.
Ask which pharmacy makes it and whether it is licensed.

sections.q: What should I check before starting either?
sections.a: Check the diagnosis, the evidence for the specific product, its FDA status, who makes it, what monitoring is planned, and what the full monthly cost includes.
checklist: Search the FDA website for the product's status.
Get pricing in writing before starting.

sections.q: Who should prescribe?
sections.a: A licensed clinician should confirm any diagnosis and prescribe. Urologists and endocrinologists treat low testosterone. State medical boards confirm licenses.
checklist: Verify the prescriber's license.
Ask whether they follow published treatment guidelines.

/uscis-medical-exam-vs-physical/.core_q: What is the core difference between a USCIS medical exam and a routine physical?
rows: Shows USCIS you meet health requirements for immigration
Checks and maintains your general health
Required tests, vaccines and screenings set by CDC instructions
Whatever you and your clinician decide

sections.q: When do I need the USCIS medical exam?
sections.a: You need the USCIS medical exam when applying to adjust status to permanent resident from inside the United States. The civil surgeon follows CDC technical instructions and completes Form I-693.
checklist: Find a civil surgeon in the USCIS locator.
Bring vaccination records and ID.

sections.q: Can a routine physical count instead?
sections.a: No. A routine physical does not meet USCIS requirements, even if it includes the same tests. Records from your regular doctor, such as vaccine history, can help the civil surgeon complete the exam.
checklist: Ask your regular doctor for a copy of your vaccine records.
Do not open the sealed I-693 envelope.

sections.q: What should I check before the exam?
sections.a: Check that the doctor is a designated civil surgeon, what the fee covers, whether vaccines and blood tests cost extra, and how long until the sealed form is ready.
checklist: Ask for the full fee in writing.
Ask how long lab results take.

sections.q: Where do I find a civil surgeon?
sections.a: Use the USCIS Find a Civil Surgeon tool and search by ZIP code. Call the office to confirm the designation, the fee and available appointments.
checklist: Search the USCIS locator by ZIP code.
Confirm the designation by phone.
